summary_html: Child safely **reunified with parent or guardian**, case closed. Federal policy treats reunification as the preferred outcome once risk factors are mitigated.
authority_html:
- **Adoption and Safe Families Act (ASFA)** — establishes reunification timelines and permanency goals  
- **SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — funds reunification services and tracks permanency outcomes

primary_citations.citation_text: Maryland - Md. Code, Family Law Article §§ 5-701 et seq. (Child Abuse and Neglect; definitions at § 5-701, mandatory reporting at §§ 5-704 and 5-705, investigation at § 5-706, appeal of findings at § 5-706.1)
Maryland - Courts & Judicial Proc. § 3-801 et seq. (CINA—Child in Need of Assistance proceedings)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Court of Special Appeals of Maryland
key_cases.holding: The court held that the juvenile court erred in finding reasonable efforts where the department made only a single vocational referral to address the father's unemployment, because the department's services must address the actual impediments to reunification.
key_cases.relevance: It defines the reasonable-efforts predicate that must be satisfied before reunification is abandoned.
key_cases.quote: the obligation to render "reasonable efforts" rests on the Department, not the parent

key_cases.holding: Resolving a split in the intermediate court, the Court held that an order waiving the department's obligation to make reasonable reunification efforts is not immediately appealable under CJP § 12-303(3)(x) because, standing alone, it does not deprive the parent of care or custody.
key_cases.relevance: A reasonable-efforts waiver is the formal end of the reunification track, and this case says when it can be challenged.
key_cases.quote: juvenile court's order waiving a department's obligation to provide reasonable reunification efforts, while leaving a custody order and permanency plan unchanged, does not deprive a parent of care or custody

key_cases.citation: No. 1609, Sept. Term 2024 (Md. App. Ct. July 1, 2025)
key_cases.holding: The court held that in CINA cases a department is generally required under the ADA to make reasonable accommodations for parents with disabilities in providing reunification services, provided the parent makes the disability and needed accommodation known, and affirmed the award of custody and guardianship to the grandparents.
key_cases.relevance: It integrates ADA accommodation into the CINA reasonable-efforts inquiry that governs reunification.
key_cases.quote: the Department is generally required under the ADA to make reasonable accommodations for parents with disabilities in rendering reunification efforts in CINA cases

key_cases.holding: The Court held that ICWA's 'active efforts' requirement is satisfied by substantive proof that the department made, and exhausted, remedial and rehabilitative efforts, and that the juvenile court need not recite the statute's wording; it reversed the intermediate court and directed that the circuit court judgment be affirmed.
key_cases.relevance: It governs when a CINA case involving an Indian child may be closed without reunification.
key_cases.quote: what is important is whether the Department in substance made active efforts to prevent the breakup of the family, whether those efforts were unsuccessful

key_cases.holding: Affirming the change of four children's permanency plans from reunification to adoption, the Court held that the reasonable-efforts requirement is case-specific and must be measured against the services actually at the department's disposal, so efforts were reasonable where the department made and pursued referrals but funding-dependent services never became available to a developmentally disabled mother.
key_cases.relevance: It defines the reasonable-efforts predicate that must be satisfied before reunification ceases to be the plan.
key_cases.quote: We shall hold that the "reasonable efforts" requirement is case-specific, and must be considered in light of the services at the Department's disposal.

key_cases.case_name: In re Adoption/Guardianship of Cadence B.
key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed a change of permanency plan from reunification to open adoption, holding that the juvenile court did not abuse its discretion in ending reunification efforts where the father had willfully absented himself from meaningful contact and the child was bonded to caregivers willing to provide a permanent home.
key_cases.relevance: It states when the statutory presumption favoring reunification is overcome and the reunification track may properly be abandoned.
key_cases.quote: if there are weighty circumstances indicating that reunification with the parent is not in the child's best interest, the court should modify the permanency plan to a more appropriate arrangement

extended_foster_care_age: Up to the 21st birthday, and only while the young person meets one of five conditions: completing secondary education or a program leading to an equivalent credential; enrolled in an institution providing post-secondary or vocational education; participating in a program or activity designed to promote or remove barriers to employment; employed at least 80 hours per month; or incapable of any of those due to a medical condition documented in the case plan (COMAR 07.02.11.04B). Not eligible for out-of-home placement if married, in the military, or not complying with those conditions (COMAR 07.02.11.04C). Re-entry: the juvenile court has jurisdiction over a former CINA whose commitment to the local department was rescinded after age 18 but before age 20 years 6 months and who did not exit foster care due to reunification, adoption, guardianship, marriage, or uniformed services duty, and that jurisdiction continues until age 21 (Md. Code, Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 3-804(b)(2) and (c)).

common_failures: Failure to prove unfitness by clear and convincing evidence
Santosky v. Kramer standard not met
